The support of the distribution of $X = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\beta_n}{3^n}$, where each $\beta_n \in \{0, 2\}$, is precisely the **Cantor set**.

**Proof.** Writing $\beta_n = 2b_n$ with $b_n \in \{0,1\}$, we have
$$X = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2b_n}{3^n} = 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{b_n}{3^n}.$$
The set of all possible values is exactly the set of numbers in $[0,1]$ admitting a ternary (base-3) expansion using only the digits $0$ and $2$ — i.e., the classical middle-thirds Cantor set $C$.

Indeed, at stage $k$ of the Cantor construction, the remaining $2^k$ intervals consist precisely of those numbers whose first $k$ ternary digits belong to $\{0,2\}$. The partial sums $X_k = \sum_{n=1}^{k}\frac{\beta_n}{3^n}$ select one such interval of length $3^{-k}$, and $X = \lim_k X_k$ lies in the intersection $\bigcap_k C_k = C$. Conversely every point of $C$ is realized by some choice of digits, so the support equals $C$.

The Lebesgue measure of $C$ is
$$\lambda(C) = \lim_{k\to\infty} 2^k \cdot 3^{-k} = \lim_{k\to\infty}\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^k = 0.$$

Therefore the maximum Lebesgue measure of the support of the distribution of $X$ is $\boxed{0}$.

### PROOF COMPLETE

This is the Cantor distribution. The support is the Cantor set, which has Lebesgue measure 0.

So the maximum Lebesgue measure of the support is 0.

The support is the Cantor set (all numbers in [0,1] with ternary expansion using only digits 0 and 2). The Lebesgue measure of the Cantor set is 0.

### PROOF COMPLETE
